Situation1: They send an occasional text to check in with their parents over the weekend.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story: It was Saturday afternoon when my phone buzzed with a message from my mom: “Hope you’re having a good weekend. Miss you!” I glanced at it, guilt pricking at me—I hadn’t called home in over a week, and I knew my parents expected at least a quick check-in. I started typing a reply, but before I could hit send, another notification popped up: a community leader tagging me in a post about a discriminatory incident at a local business. As an advocate, I was expected to act fast, mobilize support, and get the word out. My inbox filled with messages from colleagues and community members, all looking to me for a response. I stared at my mom’s text, then at the urgent calls for action. My heart pounded as I weighed the comfort my parents sought against the responsibility I felt to speak out. Both roles demanded my attention, but I only had so much to give.
